analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal for an employer to recognize a union without a government-run secret ballot election.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. Lindsey Graham with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate labor committee and died there when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current labor law, a union can become the workers' legal representative in two ways: winning an election run by the National Labor Relations Board, or by showing an employer signed authorization cards from a majority of employees — a path known as card check. Card check is faster, and workers can unionize without the long, contested campaign period that a formal election involves. This bill would make card check illegal: an employer who recognized a union without a government-run secret ballot election, and a union that pressured an employer to do so, would both be committing an unfair labor practice. Existing union contracts would be left alone.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers facing organizing drives gain: under current law they can be legally recognized as dealing with a union once a majority of employees sign cards, which can happen in weeks. By making a government election the only route to recognition, the bill would ensure every organizing drive goes through a process that takes months, during which employers may hold mandatory meetings and campaign against the union. It also protects employers from being pressed into a card-check agreement. The bill's stated benefit for workers is protection from union pressure, since a signed card is cast openly rather than in private.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unfair labor practice for an employer to recognize or bargain with a union that has not won a majority in an NLRB-conducted secret ballot election.
Makes it an unfair labor practice for a union to press an employer to recognize it without such an election, eliminating card-check agreements.
Requires the NLRB to rewrite its regulations within six months to fit the new election requirement, and leaves existing bargaining relationships grandfathered.

analysis.who_pays: Employees who want a union lose the fastest, least contentious way to get one. NLRB elections are typically held weeks or months after a petition is filed, and during that window an employer can legally hold mandatory anti-union meetings and campaign against representation. Requiring an election in every case makes successful unionization harder, and research consistently finds that unionized jobs pay more and offer better benefits than comparable non-union jobs. Workers who prefer a union would also lose the option of asking their employer to simply accept a demonstrated majority.

drawbacks.text: The bill would eliminate card-check recognition entirely, removing the fastest route to union representation; workers could get a union only through the slower NLRB election process, during which employers are free to campaign against the union, and the bill contains no new safeguards against that employer pressure.

Supporters' good-faith case: union card drives can involve peer and organizer pressure, and a private signed card is not a private vote; the bill's findings argue that only a government-supervised secret ballot is free of coercion, and employers could no longer be pushed into recognizing a union without one.

By barring unions from even asking employers to recognize a majority sign-up, the bill forecloses a voluntary private agreement between an employer and its employees' chosen representative, even when no worker objects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated benefit — protecting workers from union pressure via a secret ballot — is the strongest good-faith case, and secret ballot elections are a genuine democratic safeguard. But the bill's practical effect is to shut down the fastest and least conflict-ridden path to union recognition while leaving untouched the employer advantages in the election process, so the cost (harder, slower unionization and the wage and benefit differences that come with it) falls on workers rather than being balanced by any protection against employer coercion. It also bans one tool for both sides while leaving management's tools intact.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee with no cosponsors, and nothing ever happened to it before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 9, 2004, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearings, no committee vote, no floor action. The 108th Congress ended January 3, 2005, and the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers and unions were no worse off than before, since the law was unchanged; employers got the outcome they would have wanted without needing the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The law stayed unchanged; employers face no new bar to card check

for.name: Sen. Lindsey Graham
for.role: U.S. Senator from South Carolina (bill sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require NLRB-supervised secret ballot elections before union recognition.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape beyond the Republican sponsor cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would take away labor's quickest path to recognition, leaving employers facing only the slower NLRB election process, in which they can lawfully campaign against the union while the election is pending. That makes it harder and more expensive for employees to unionize, which in turn weakens workers' leverage over pay and conditions.

Card check is one of the main ways unions win representation at non-union workplaces, and this bill would outlaw both employers' use of it and unions' efforts to obtain it. Existing bargaining relationships would be grandfathered, so the loss falls on future organizing.
